evidence: Abstract, Secs.3-5 (pp.1-9): SHAP ranking variability across resampling/seeds and a robust metric (RoSHAP)
problem: SHAP values and rankings vary across train-test splits, seeds and fitting procedures but are reported as fixed.
method: Bootstrap resampling and refitting; kernel density estimation of SHAP-score distributions (with an asymptotic Gaussian approximation); RoSHAP combines activity, strength and stability into a robust ranking criterion.
data: Simulations and real datasets incl. high-dimensional gene-expression data (Fig.1) and an image example (Sec.5).
evaluation: Ranking stability across repeated analyses; recovery of signal vs chance-selected features in simulations.
findings: RoSHAP improves interpretation stability and separates consistent signals from chance-selected features (Sec.6).
limitations: Authors: bootstrap cost; extension to model-level randomness left for future work (p.9).
qa_notes: Q3 dataset details partly in appendix; Q4 compared with standard SHAP only; Q10 bootstrap replicates.; Q7=0.5: original appraisal retained; supporting extracted limitations: Authors: bootstrap cost; extension to model-level randomness left for future work (p.9).

evidence: Executive summary, Secs.3-5, 9 (pp.5-18,35): impossibility of stable SHAP rankings under collinearity; experiments on 11 datasets and a 77-dataset survey
problem: Retraining the same model with a different seed can invert which correlated feature SHAP ranks as most important.
method: Proves that no feature ranking can be faithful, stable and complete under collinearity; quantitative bounds for gradient boosting, Lasso, neural networks and random forests; DASH (ensemble-averaged SHAP) as resolution; Lean 4 formalisation (305 theorems).
data: Survey of 77 public datasets; experiments across 11 datasets and 3 GBDT implementations; financial case studies (p.6).
evaluation: Flip rates of within-group rankings, expected Spearman ranking stability, bootstrap 95% CIs over 10 trials (p.18); SNR-based flip-rate formula (R2 = 0.94 on Breast Cancer, p.35).
findings: 68% of 77 datasets show attribution instability; for collinear pairs the ranking is close to a coin flip; the attribution ratio diverges as 1/(1-rho^2) for gradient boosting but converges for random forests; DASH yields stable rankings (pp.5-15).
limitations: Authors: the result concerns the single-model paradigm; conditional SHAP does not escape it (p.7). Ours: preprint; very long theoretical document.
repro: Code and Lean proofs: github.com/DrakeCaraker/dash-impossibility-lean and dash-shap.

evidence: Secs.3-5 (pp.3-11): run-to-run stability of LIME/SHAP rankings on four tabular datasets
read_from: Preprint arXiv:2608.02697 (accepted at EXPLAINS 2026 per arXiv listing)
problem: Stochastic components make attribution rankings vary between runs; how far down a ranking can be trusted?
method: Distribution-based framework: attribution distributions over repeated runs; pairwise separability of adjacent features (continuous Jaccard distance) defines the largest reliable rank (k-stability); explainers compared by the proportion of instances where one is more stable.
data: Diabetes, Heart Disease, Mobile and Churn tabular benchmarks (p.7).
evaluation: k-stability over 50 instances x 50 runs per explainer (LIME, SHAP, DiCE, random baseline); +/-2 sigma/sqrt(n) intervals; sensitivity to number of runs (pp.7-10).
findings: SHAP was quasi-deterministic (perfect stability) on Churn and Diabetes; LIME rankings were reliable only for the first few positions; the metric was not very sensitive to the number of runs (pp.8-11).
limitations: Authors: controlled tabular classification only; design choices of the metric (p.11).
repro: Code to be released upon acceptance (p.6).
qa_notes: Q8 code not yet released; Q10 50 runs per instance.

evidence: Abstract, Secs.4-5 (pp.1,10-14): variability of LIME/SHAP via Weight of Evidence on tabular Titanic and synthetic data
problem: Attribution scores alone do not show how well an explainer aligns with a reference hypothesis or how variable it is.
method: Weight-of-Evidence hypothesis-testing framework for feature-importance methods with theory linking WoE to attribution variance; LIME and SHAP explaining a random forest, 50 runs on 50 instances with top-k (k=3).
data: Titanic (domain-knowledge hypotheses) and a synthetic classification dataset with known informative features (pp.10-11).
evaluation: WoE vs ground truth and vs model-derived hypotheses; coefficient of variation of WoE across runs.
findings: LIME gave variable WoE across runs, whereas SHAP was deterministic (23 instances woe=+inf, 27 woe=-inf on Titanic); WoE estimates were consistent (80% of CVs between 0 and 0.3) (pp.10,14).
limitations: Authors: several design choices (uniform prior, hard hypothesis matching) not claimed optimal (p.14).
repro: Preprocessing and hyperparameters deferred to the final version; no code link.
qa_notes: Q2/Q3 details deferred; Q4 limited baselines; Q6 small experiments; Q8 none.; Q10: Sections5.2 and5.4 report50runs on50instances and sensitivity to5–100runs; random seeds or RNG control are not reported in the inspected v2 (https://arxiv.org/html/2609.00090v2). Partial credit for repetition counts.

evidence: Abstract and experiments (pp.1-8): Kernel SHAP run-to-run instability and a fully stable variant on tabular datasets
read_from: arXiv:2312.12115 version of the AAAI 2024 paper (doi 10.1609/aaai.v38i12.29208)
problem: Kernel SHAP gives different explanations for the same input across executions because of stochastic neighbour (coalition) selection.
method: ST-SHAP: deterministic, layer-wise neighbour selection (layer-1 coalitions) that removes sampling instability while keeping fidelity; theoretical analysis of layer-1 attribution scores.
data: Tabular datasets incl. Adult, Dry Bean, Movie and Credit Card (Table 4).
evaluation: Jaccard coefficient of non-zero feature sets across repeated executions; Kendall's tau and R2 vs exact SHAP values.
findings: ST-SHAP achieved full stability without compromising fidelity; layer-1 scores stayed close to exact SHAP values (Table 4; Conclusion).
limitations: Authors: future work on other explainers. Ours: run-to-run stability only (no input perturbation).

evidence: Abstract and Sec.5 (pp.1,9-10): Monte-Carlo variability of Shapley estimates reduced with control variates on tabular data
problem: Sampling approximations of Shapley values carry considerable Monte-Carlo uncertainty.
method: ControlSHAP: control variates based on Taylor (linear/quadratic) approximations of the model for both independent and correlated feature settings.
data: Simulated correlated data; UCI Portuguese bank, German credit, census income and breast-cancer subtyping (p.9).
evaluation: Variance reduction of Shapley estimates and number of ranking changes across repetitions.
findings: ControlSHAP reduces Monte Carlo variability, with the reduction depending on model, dataset and feature-dependence assumption; selected cases reach about 90%, rather than a uniform 80–95% across settings (Secs.5–6).
limitations: Authors: the correlated case needs accurate pre-computed matrices; LIME and distillation trees are also unstable (p.14).
qa_notes: Q7 limited; Q10 repeated estimation runs.

evidence: Abstract and Sec.6 (pp.1,11-17): probabilistic-Lipschitz robustness of LIME/IG/SmoothGrad/SHAP with tabular XOR and Iris (plus MNIST)
problem: Which explainer is most robust, and how does network smoothness relate to explanation robustness?
method: Lower bounds on probabilistic Lipschitzness of Integrated Gradients, LIME and SmoothGrad; normalised astuteness metric; link between a network's local Lipschitz constant and its stable rank.
data: XOR, Iris (tabular) and MNIST; MLPs with 2-16 layers (p.12).
evaluation: Normalised astuteness of explainers; stable rank as heuristic.
findings: Integrated gradients were less robust than SHAP or LIME; stable rank agreed with normalised astuteness (Sec.7).
limitations: Authors: dependence on the Lipschitz constant; efficacy of stable rank needs more study (pp.2,17). Ours: neural networks only; toy tabular data.
qa_notes: Q3 toy datasets; Q6 limited empirical scope; Q8 none; Q10 sampling not detailed.

evidence: Abstract and Sec.5.2 (pp.1,7-13): stability of SHAP and other XAI rankings under test-data perturbation on tabular diabetes data
problem: How reliable and stable are XAI methods when test data are perturbed?
method: Pipeline with LGBM, MLP, decision tree and KNN; test data perturbed at increasing levels; feature-relevance ranks from Dalex, Eli5, eXirt, Lofo and SHAP compared; IRT-based eXirt reliability analysis.
evaluation: Spearman correlation and bump charts of feature ranks across perturbation levels; Friedman-Nemenyi tests for model performance (p.9).
findings: Most XAI methods, including SHAP, changed rankings under perturbation; eXirt identified less reliable models (Sec.5).
limitations: Ours: single small dataset; preprint; perturbation design loosely specified.
qa_notes: Q2/Q3 limited detail; Q6 descriptive; Q7 none explicit; Q10 perturbation levels but no repetitions reported.
